subject: Geography
description: Eight major soil types of India — distribution, characteristics, suitable crops

questions.stem: The most widely distributed soil in India by area is:
questions.explanation: Alluvial soil — covers ~46% of India's total area. Found in the Indo-Gangetic plain, brahmaputra valley, coastal belts of east coast (deltas of Mahanadi, Krishna, Godavari, Kaveri), Narmada and Tapi valleys. Two sub-types: Khadar (newer alluvium, fine-grained, fertile, replenished annually by floods) and Bhangar (older alluvium, contains kankar/calcareous nodules). Highly fertile — supports rice, wheat, sugarcane, oilseeds, pulses. Black soil is 2nd most extensive (~16%).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Black soil (Regur) is best suited for the cultivation of:

options.option_text: Cotton — hence also called 'black cotton soil'

questions.explanation: Black soil — formed from weathering of Deccan Trap basalts. Rich in iron, magnesium, lime, alumina; deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, organic matter. Found in Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat (Saurashtra), parts of TN, AP, Karnataka. High moisture-retention capacity due to clayey texture (>50% clay). Develops cracks in summer = self-ploughing. Best for cotton, also good for jowar, wheat, sugarcane, oilseeds, citrus. Trap option Tea — actually grown on red/laterite soils; Coffee — laterite/red soils.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Laterite soil — typical of high-rainfall plateau regions — gets its red colour from:
questions.explanation: Laterite forms in tropical regions with high rainfall — silica leaches out leaving Fe and Al oxides. Fe oxide → red/brick colour ('latericius' = brick in Latin). Found in Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Goa), Eastern Ghats (Odisha), parts of Assam, Meghalaya, Chhattisgarh. Generally infertile (low N, P, K), acidic; useful for cashew, rubber, coffee, tea, coconut. Hardens on exposure → used as building bricks. Same root word 'laterite' derives.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Match the soil type with its dominant region — which pairing is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Arid / desert soil is found in RAJASTHAN (Thar desert), Haryana's southern parts, Gujarat's Kutch — NOT Punjab plains (which have rich alluvial soil from Indus tributaries). Desert soils are sandy, low in clay/humus, alkaline, saline; need irrigation + nitrogen. Indira Gandhi Canal has converted parts of western Rajasthan into productive agricultural land. Other major Indian soil types — peaty/marshy (Kerala backwaters, Sundarbans), forest soil (humus-rich on hills), saline-alkaline (Reh — UP, Haryana, dryland Maharashtra).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Khadar and Bhangar are sub-types of which soil?
questions.explanation: Alluvial soil — divided by AGE: Khadar = newer alluvium (light-coloured, fine-grained, more fertile, replenished by annual floods, found close to rivers); Bhangar = older alluvium (darker, coarser, contains 'kankar' calcareous nodules, often raised above flood-plains, less fertile but well-drained). Khadar suits intensive cultivation; Bhangar is good for plantation / construction. Term Bhangar comes from 'bhang' meaning broken / weathered.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Soil erosion in India is most severe in which form?
questions.explanation: Water erosion — main culprit (~75% of erosion-affected area in India). Forms: sheet (uniform thin layer removal), rill (small channels), gully (deep channels — Chambal-Yamuna ravines famous), riverbank, coastal. Wind erosion mostly in Rajasthan/Gujarat (~25% of total). Total degraded land in India ~30% (ICAR-IISWC). Mitigation — afforestation, contour bunding, terrace farming, gully plugging, check dams, mulching. Watershed development is the integrated approach.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: ICAR's National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land-Use Planning (NBSS&LUP) is headquartered in:
questions.explanation: NBSS&LUP — Nagpur, Maharashtra. Established 1976 under ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research). Mandate — soil surveys at various scales (1:1M for India, district-level), classification, mapping (Soil Resource Maps of India), land-use planning. Issues 'Soil Health Card' jointly with state agriculture departments. India also has the Soil Health Card scheme (launched 2015 by PM Modi) — every farmer gets a card with soil-test results + recommendations every 2 years.

questions.stem: Saline and alkaline soils that form in poorly drained semi-arid tracts of northern India are locally known as:

options.option_text: Khadar and Bhangar (old and new alluvium types)
Bhed and Khel (local Himalayan slope terms)
Terai and Duars (Himalayan foothills belt soils)

questions.explanation: Usar (also called Kallar in Punjab) and Reh are indigenous terms for saline/alkaline soils found across UP, Haryana, and Rajasthan; capillary action draws salts to the surface in low-rainfall conditions. Khadar and Bhangar are sub-types of alluvial soil — a common distractor — but they describe age, not salinity.

questions.stem: Laterite, being soft when freshly quarried but hardening on air exposure, has been used as a traditional building material for houses and temples predominantly in which Indian state?

options.option_text: Tamil Nadu, renowned for its granite temple architecture
Kerala, where laterite blocks are a primary construction material
Odisha, famous for its fine-grained sandstone temples
Rajasthan, where marble and red sandstone dominate structures

questions.explanation: The word 'laterite' itself comes from Latin 'later' (brick), coined because Kerala's laterite was quarried into blocks for construction. Its unique property — soft and carvable when wet, hard after drying — makes it ideal. Tamil Nadu, Odisha, and Rajasthan have distinct stone traditions but do not rely primarily on laterite blocks.

questions.stem: Which clay mineral is chiefly responsible for the dramatic shrink-swell behaviour, deep seasonal cracking, and high plasticity of black cotton soil (Regur)?

options.option_text: Kaolinite, a non-swelling 1:1 clay dominant in laterite soils
Illite, a moderately swelling clay common in temperate-region soils
Chlorite, a magnesium-iron clay found in metamorphic rock zones

questions.explanation: Montmorillonite (smectite) has expandable 2:1 lattice layers that absorb water between sheets, causing volume changes of up to 100%. This gives Vertisols (black soils) their hallmark cracks in summer and stickiness in monsoon. Kaolinite (1:1, non-swelling) dominates well-leached laterite soils — a frequent distractor because laterite is also clay-rich.

questions.stem: Red soils of the Deccan and peninsular India are naturally poor in productivity. Which combination of nutrient deficiencies is most characteristically associated with them?

options.option_text: Deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic humus content
Deficient in potassium, calcium, and manganese availability
Deficient in iron, copper, and molybdenum micronutrients
Deficient in sulfur, boron, and magnesium compound levels

questions.explanation: Red soils are porous and drain rapidly, preventing humus accumulation. They are low in nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic matter but are not iron-deficient — the high ferric oxide content is precisely what colours them red. Option C is the most tempting wrong choice because iron is visually dominant, but it is present in excess, not deficit.

questions.stem: Peaty (organic) soils form in waterlogged conditions with high organic accumulation. Which region–characteristic pairing for India's peaty soils is CORRECT?

options.option_text: Kuttanad in Kerala — below mean sea-level paddy cultivation
Rann of Kutch in Gujarat — seasonal saline mudflat terrain
Thar Desert in Rajasthan — sandy arid and wind-eroded soils
Chotanagpur Plateau in Jharkhand — thin laterite-type soils

questions.explanation: Kuttanad (Kerala) lies 1–2 m below mean sea level and its perennially waterlogged paddyfields overlie thick peaty, humus-rich organic soils — one of India's most distinctive agricultural landscapes. The Rann of Kutch has saline (not peaty) soils; Chotanagpur has laterite soils. Students often confuse 'marshy' with 'saline', making B the most common wrong pick.

questions.stem: Under the USDA Soil Taxonomy adopted by NBSS&LUP for classifying India's soils, which soil order accounts for the single largest share of India's geographical area?

options.option_text: Vertisols — the USDA order that covers black cotton soil belts
Alfisols — moderately leached soils of red-and-yellow regions
Inceptisols — young soils with weakly developed horizon profiles
Entisols — very recent soils with virtually no profile development

questions.explanation: NBSS&LUP mapping shows Inceptisols cover ~39% of India's area, incorporating much of the Indo-Gangetic alluvial plains and parts of the Deccan; Entisols (~28%) rank second covering fresh alluvium and coastal sands; Alfisols (~13.5%) rank third. Vertisols cover only ~8.5%. Entisols are the most tempting wrong answer because alluvial soils are 'recent', but the deeper IGP soils with any horizon development classify as Inceptisols.

questions.stem: A soil exhibits 'gilgai' micro-relief (alternating mounds and hollows), opens into deep polygonal cracks in summer, and requires minimal tillage for sustained productivity. What is the self-regulating mechanism that maintains its fertility without ploughing?

options.option_text: Iron chelation continuously recirculates phosphorus to upper layers
Annual flood events deposit a fresh organic horizon every season
Shrink-swell cycling buries surface crop residue into deep cracks
Dense mycorrhizal networks compensate for structural compaction loss

questions.explanation: Vertisols (black soils) contain montmorillonite clay that swells when wet and shrinks in the dry season, opening cracks up to 1 m deep. Surface organic residues and fine soil fall into these cracks; when rains rewet the soil, swelling closes the cracks and buries this material — effectively self-ploughing and self-mulching. The gilgai pattern arises from differential heaving at crack margins. Option B (flooding) misleads because black-soil regions are semi-arid, not flood-prone like Kuttanad.
